sections.text: A Process is defined as an execution environment with private virtual memory space and system resources. Each process maintains its own page tables, file descriptor table, and security credentials. In contrast, a Thread refers to a schedulable execution unit within a process that shares memory and address space with sibling threads. The primary advantage of multi-threading is reduced context switch overhead compared to inter-process switching.

Virtual Memory is a memory management architecture that creates an idealized abstraction of storage resources. The Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual page numbers (VPN) into physical frame numbers (PFN) using Page Tables. A Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) acts as a high-speed hardware cache for virtual-to-physical address mappings. When a process requests an address not currently mapped in physical RAM, a Page Fault exception is triggered.

A Deadlock occurs when processes hold resources and wait indefinitely for resources held by other processes. The four Coffman conditions required for deadlock are: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. A Semaphore is an integer synchronization variable used to control concurrent access to common shared resources. A Mutex provides mutual exclusion locks guaranteeing that only one thread can execute a critical section at any given time.

Round Robin Scheduling is a preemptive scheduling algorithm where each process is assigned a fixed time quantum. Shortest Job First (SJF) is an optimal scheduling policy that minimizes average turnaround time for a batch of jobs. Priority Inversion occurs when a lower-priority task holds a shared lock needed by a higher-priority task.

CS301 Operating Systems covers core kernel abstractions, concurrency, scheduling, virtual memory, and storage. The final grade is weighted as follows: Midterm Exam 30%, Final Comprehensive Examination 40%, Programming Homework Assignments 30%.
